description: Somos Chenque in Space, Nuestras solución al problema se trata de una web el cual visualizara e informara los datos geológicos y meteorológicos de la zona/región de interés del publico. La importancia de esta información yace en las estrategias de rotación y recomendaciones que brindara la web para los cultivos de sus usuarios
summary:
Great Rotation is a web decision-support tool that helps Argentine farmers choose crop rotations that protect their soil and adapt to a changing climate.

A farmer draws their field on a map, confirms the current crop (pre-filled from INTA’s National Crop Map), and ranks their priorities: saving water, improving soil, profit or lower risk. In the background, our backend analyzes the field with NASA Earth observations: NASA POWER climate since 1981, GPM IMERG rainfall, SMAP soil moisture, Sentinel-2/Landsat and MODIS NDVI, and SRTM slope, combined with SoilGrids soil data. It detects the field’s existing rotation from seven seasons of crop history. Then it compares that rotation with two alternatives using a FAO-56 daily water balance, nitrogen, crop residue, bare-soil days and frost and heat risk. Each strategy explains why it was suggested, the evidence, its benefits, its data gaps and its risks for local review. A public dashboard also shows rainfall, heat and soil-moisture anomalies and long-term trends for all 24 provinces, plus an in-app soil-moisture sensor alert.

Rainfall is becoming less predictable and soils are degrading in one of the world’s largest grain producers. Great Rotation turns decades of NASA data into clear, honest guidance that supports farmer’s judgment rather than replacing it.
details:
What it does: Great Rotation is a web app that helps Argentine farmers compare crop-rotation strategies using NASA data. A public dashboard covers all 24 provinces. It shows rainfall, soil-moisture, temperature and NDVI anomalies (GPM IMERG, SMAP, NASA POWER, MODIS) and long-term trends since 1981.

How it works: A farmer draws their field and confirms the current crop, which we suggest automatically from INTA’s National Crop Map. They also enter irrigation and rank their priorities: water, soil, profit or risk. A background job uses Google Earth Engine to extract Sentinel-2 NDVI, seven seasons of crop history, SRTM slope and SoilGrids soil data, plus NASA POWER climate.

We infer the field’s existing rotation and compare it with two alternatives. Each one is simulated with a daily FAO-56 water balance plus nitrogen, residue, bare-soil days, frost and heat risk, pest-cycle breaks and profit, weighted by the farmer’s priorities. Each strategy explains why it was suggested, its evidence, benefits, information gaps and risks for local review. A sensor API triggers soil-moisture alerts.

Impact: Droughts, erratic rainfall and soybean-heavy rotations are degrading soils in a major grain producer. We turn decades of NASA observations into guidance a farmer can read in minutes. It supports their judgment rather than replacing it.

Tools: Next.js (TypeScript) on Vercel, FastAPI (Python) on Railway, Supabase Postgres/PostGIS, Google Earth Engine and an LLM that only writes plain-language explanations.

Creativity: We read each field’s real rotation from satellite crop maps instead of asking the farmer for it. We clearly separate field-level data (“your field”, 10–30 m) from regional data (“your area”, 9–50 km). The rules are explainable, with no black-box machine learning.

Factors considered: Data resolution and transparency (source and date always shown), regional diversity, agronomic realism (FAO-56 coefficients, Argentine crop calendars), simple farmer-friendly design and low-cost hosting.

SI/AI Acknowledgment: An LLM is used strictly to translate deterministic FAO-56 simulation outputs into plain-language explanations and power a domain-bounded agronomic chat; AI coding assistants were also used during development.
